messages.body_plain:
Brian

There are more layers to the onion than there first appeared with multiple species and geographic strata entering the picture.  Let's work through the elements.

First, apologies for two errors on my part:
You are correct that average detectability is 0.4 not 0.04, my mistake.
Second error of mine was to not provide complete syntax for the call to dht2.  The error message returned from dht2 was asking that you provide your obs.table, sample.table and region.table data frames for arguments "observation", "transect" and "geo_strat" respectively; with "year" being treated as a stratification covariate.  With the news that there exists genuine geographic stratification in the survey design, this approach is no longer valid unless you intend to conduct three separate analyses, one for each geographic stratum.  If you are happy to conduct separate analyses for each stratum, then consider the flatfile approach described below.

With regard to birds occurring in groups, your data can be organised in the "flatfile" format, including an additional field that must be named "size" for group size.  There is no necessity that the region.table, sample.table and obs.table style of data input be used (despite the impression given by the documentation for the ds() function).  Adopting the flatfile data format ought to smooth your analysis of multiple datasets.

>From what I gather, the analysis you wish to conduct would produce year- and stratum-specific estimates of density taking into account group size for HAAM (and nine other species).

I believe the "proper" way to do this would be to use two-level stratification.  Theoretically, dht2 was designed to accept syntax such as this:

strat_formula=~Year+Region.Label

however this is untested.  What you want is on the edge of what the Distance package is currently able to do.  If you are under time pressure to complete the analyses, you might need to take a more 'production line' approach filtering data by year and strata, fitting detection functions and producing abundance estimates.  For data-poor species, you might need a more elegant approach treating either year or strata as covariates, bringing you back to your original question, where you may be able to employ dht2.  Feel free to correspond further off list.

So my question is, if it is not through a regression line, what is the "expected" cluster size shown in the results section of MRDS?

Many thanks

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ana, (list)

Summary: expected cluster size is estimated number of individuals
divided by estimated number of clusters.

Longer answer - first some notation:
Let i = 1, ... , n index the observations; let z_i be the vector of
detection function covariates for observation i, which might include s_i
the observed cluster size for that observation.  Assume we've fitted a
detection function using MCDS or MRDS and that \hat{p}(z_i) is the
estimated detection probability for the ith observation given its
covariates z_i.

Then, the estimated number of individuals in the covered area (i.e., the
transects) is given by the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator

\hat{N} = sum_{i=1}^n \frac{s_i}{\hat{p}(z_i)}

(in case you're not used to LaTeX notation that's the sum over all
observations of s_i divided by \hat{p}(z_i)).

The estimated number of clusters is given by

\hat{N_c} = sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\hat{p}(z_i)}

(similar but the sum of 1 divided by \hat{p}(z_i)).

The estimated expected cluster size is simply \hat{N_c} divided by \hat{N}.

So, it's not really that the abundance estimates are calculated using
the expected cluster size - instead it's the expected cluster size is
calculated using the abundance estimates!

Hope this helps! Len

messages.body_plain:
Nope, it's not the same as using mean group size.

(In formulae:

\hat{N} = sum_{i=1}^n \frac{s_i}{\hat{p}(z_i)}

i.e., the sum of s_i/p(z_i), summed over all observed animals

is not the same as

\hat{N} = \frac{sum_{i=1}^n s_i}{n}  \frac{1}{\hat{p}(z_i)}

i.e., mean group size times sum of 1/p(z_i) summed over all observed animals

unless all of the z_i's are the same - i.e., no covariates.)

You can think of it as using an estimate of the population mean group
size, rather than the observed mean group size.

Best, Len

Hi all,

I have a question about how to include points in which there were no detections when distances are binned.

I am working with point count data (so, point transects), attempting to estimate bird abundances. The distances are binned, however, because I am doing this species by species, there will be many points in which a given species was not detected. Additionally, there are a number of points in which no birds were detected. I want to include these points in the abundance analysis to get accurate detection probabilities, but I am not sure how to code the 'distbegin' and 'distend' columns for these points. When I attempt to create bins for these data and include points in which a species was not detected, with an NA in the distance column, I get this error:

Error in create.bins(all.data, c(0, 50, 100)) :
  Some distances are NA, can't create bins.

This seems like a potentially common question with an easy solution, so I apologize if this has been answered previously, but I've been struggling to find an answer

Thanks for any help.
Best,
Sam

> Dear Group

I calculated density and abundance using the Distance software and would now like to understand what factors are involved in the observed gazelle distribution. I understand I can use habitat covariates using using distance software, but thought a better way would be to create a resource selection function using the gazelle point data and a used / available design. I read two papers that did this some time ago by Brian Manly (2002) and L. Kastdalen (2003), but have not seen the method used since then, which makes me suspicious that I am missing something. Is there any reason why I should not use this method for data collected during distance surveys?
>

>
> Method for gaining available sample (Kastdalen et al. 2003)
> To correct for the unequal detection of gazelle according to distance from the observer, we created a random selection of available points using ArcGIS within a 500m buffer from the transect lines, indicating the cut point from the detection probability function. For each random point generated we then estimated the probability that it should be sampled according to the detection probability function for the lines.
>
> Kastdalen, L., Pedersen, H. C., Fjone, G., & Andreassen, H. P. (2003). Combining resource selection functions and distance sampling: an example with willow ptarmigan. Proceedings of 1st International Conference on Resource Selection by Animals, Laramie, Wyoming.

messages.subject: Data structure for DSM
messages.subject_clean: Data structure for DSM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Listfolk,

I am just getting started with the DSM function in R, but have had a bit of experience with Distance by now. Currently, I am trying to structure my data and model appropriately, but since I am dealing with a data set that doesn't easily lend itself to geographically distributed abundance estimates I would love to get some input.

Survey design

Data collection was done over 7 years, twice per season for the 3 discernible seasons. While surveys were conducted on trails that cover the majority of the site, vegetation plots were only done at points every 2 km along this trail. Thus I created 1km length plots, centered on the location of the vegetation plot and sampled all observation within those plots. Each observation received the covariates for that plot at that time (given covariates such as NDVI change over time). Thus we have 41 samples made over 7 years for each of 213 plots.

So, I don’t have a typical distance sampling structure but I think it can be made to work given the right formatting of the data and reference data frames (such as observation and segment table...). However I have been scratching my head on how this should actually look.

Data structure

At present the key columns are presented below as follows:

  size distance(m) Sample.Label object Effort SURV.GR YEAR

1    0     1001          1-12      1   1000       6 2013

2    0     1001          1-10      2   1000       5 2013

3    10    89            1-1       3   1000       1 2012

4    0     1001          1-11      4   1000       6 2013

5    2     130           1-13      5   1000       7 2014

6    0     1001          1-14      6   1000       7 2014

size = cluster/group size

distance(m) = perpendicular distance to each observation. Where size=0, I replaced NAs with a large number (1001) which is well beyond any reasonable truncation distance for my study as I wasn’t sure if NAs would cause the observations to be removed (this was simply an idea not sure how dsm actually handles these rows yet?).

Sample.Label is a combination of survey number (1-41) and plotID (1-213) giving 8733 unique values. All 8733 combinations are represented in Sample.Label giving counts for size or a 0 where no observations were made on that survey, multiple rows for the same Sample.Label are also possible when multiple observations were made in the same plot on the same survey. Aggregation is not possible to preserve the distance measurement.

Effort = plot length (as described each of the 213 plots were 1km long).

Object = a unique identifier for each observation.

SURV.GR <http://SURV.GR> = survey group where the two surveys per season were grouped together (i.e. we made 21 groups from 41 individuals surveys, last group contains just 1). This is used as a random effect.

In addition I have complimentary columns for each of my environmental covariates such as "Group1" and "Group2" that refer to percentage cover of that vegetative community (remember the value of these covariates are assigned to observations based on the plot in which they were observed).

Model structure

Some preliminary models have the structure:

mod1 <-dsm(formula = abundance.est ~ s(Group1, k=10) + s(Group2, k=10) + s(SURV.GR, YEAR, PlotID, bs="re")

               , family = nb()

               , engine = "gam"

               , ddf.obj=impala.ddf

               , segment.data=seg.data

               , observation.data=impala300

               , method="REML")

Some comments here:

I am using a negative binomial distribution to model my over-dispersed, count data
My response is abundance.est since my detection function also has covariates
I have not scaled the variables as I have read this can lead to erroneous outputs in conjunction with the smoothing s() function in R
I have not included and s(x,y) term
I have added (I hope!!) a term that states PlotID is nested in YEAR which is nested in SURV.GR <http://SURV.GR> as a random effect

My overall goal from this analysis is to estimate abundance at the plot level, when I get to the stage of using predict for the GAM I also hope that I can show the relationships predicted by the best fitted model with each of my covariates to infer habitat preferences

Questions

Finally, my questions are:
How should a prediction data grid look in a case where I only know the value of environmental variables within the discrete plots?
Have I structured my data correctly to get at plot abundances and to infer habitat type preferences?
Is the reason for including an s(x,y) term (as per the vignette example) simply to allow for the geographical visualisation of the response variable?
Does the structure of my model formula correctly reflect the intended nested structure of my data as a random effect?

Any and all comments are truly welcome, thank you for your time.

Note: I have also posted the part about nested random effect terms in GAM formulas on cross validate, see this link <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/431692/how-does-random-variable-nesting-in-gams-work-mgcv>

messages.subject_clean: Calculating ESW with both left and right truncation
messages.body_plain:
Hi there!

I've been doing some literature scouring and haven't been able to find what I'm looking for so I thought I might try here.

I am estimating detection functions using the ds() function in R package Distance for some aerial survey data, which requires the use of both a left and a right truncation. I have my models all selected but am now looking to calculate the ESW and have am struggling to determine the best approach. I understand that ESW = Probability of Detection (Pa) * Right truncation distance (W), but I'm not sure how the left truncation distance comes in to play.

My coworker and I have come up with a couple of possible equations:

     1)   Pa * (Right_Trunc - Left_Trunc)

     2)   (Pa * Right_Trunc) - Left_Trunc

     3)   (Pa * Right_Trunc) / (Right_Trunc - Left_Trunc) from Supplementary Materials from Laake Jeff, Guenzel Richard J., Bengtson John L., Boveng Peter, Cameron Michael, Hanson M. Bradley (2008) Coping with variation in aerial survey
                                                                                       protocol for line-transect sampling. Wildlife Research 35, 289-299.

So I guess my questions are:

     1) Do we need to actually incorporate the left truncation distance in the ESW equation or is it already accounted for during the ds() determination of Pa?

     2) If we do need to account for it, are any of the above equations correct? Or, if they are not, how would you recommend correctly incorporating the left truncation?

     3) Would it be a better idea to cut out all the sightings that fall within the left truncation distance from the dataset used in the ds() modeling and bypass the need for left truncation all together?

Thank you for your help!
Lisa

Sam

Sorry my suggestion did not work.  I've done a bit more thinking and wonder if this works for you.  Treat your distance data (collected as binned) by supplying the midpoint of the distance interval.  Then provide a "cutpoints" argument to the ds() function to have the data binned for analysis.

Here is a silly example I manufactured:

d1 <- rep(0.5,24)
d2 <- rep(1.5,20)
d3 <- rep(2.5,12)
d4 <- rep(3.5,4)
dna <- rep(NA, 10)
dist <- c(d1,d2,d3,d4,dna)
t1 <- rep(1, 24)
t2 <- rep(2,20)
t3 <- rep(3,12)
t4 <- rep(4,4)
tna <- seq(from=5, to=14)
samlab <- c(t1,t2,t3,t4,tna)
area <- 10
eff <- 2
reglab <- "Fred"
mydata <- data.frame(Region.Label=reglab,
                     Area=area,
                     Sample.Label=samlab,
                     Effort=eff,
                     distance=dist)
myresult <- ds(mydata, cutpoints = c(0,1,2,3,4))

Here the entered distances (0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5) are the midpoints of the distance intervals (0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,4).  In addition to all the other silliness, I've placed all the detections for bin 1 into transect 1, bin 2 into transect 2,... and no detections in transects 5-14.  But the point is that ds() seems happy enough calling "create.bins" via the use of the "cutpoints" argument.  It is not necessary for you to call "create.bins" yourself.

See if this works for your data.

Hi Eric,

Great! That seems to work...at least I am able to get results for most species-stratum combinations.

I am still, however, running into some issues/questions about how the Distance incorporates the points in which a species was not detected (but this record needs to be included in the detection probability estimation).

Half-normal key function selected.

I thought this had to do with how the points in which the species were not detected are coded, however, some species are able to get estimates from this model, even when they also include points in which the species was not detected.

Any thoughts on this?

Thanks again,
Sam

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Data structure for DSM
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Data structure for DSM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick, hi listfolks,

To your questions:

1. How should a prediction data grid look in a case where I only know

the value of environmental variables within the discrete plots?

- In general, your prediction grid should consist of one row for each
place you'd like to predict. The columns should be the covariates in the
dsm, plus the area of that cell. If you have 10 plots, you're prediction
grid will have 10 rows. You can only make predictions where you have all
the covariates that were in your model. The DSM vignette at
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/mexico-analysis.html gives and
example of a more complex prediction frame for a contiguous area.

2. Have I structured my data correctly to get at plot abundances and to
infer habitat type preferences?

  - You don't seem to present all the data.frames you need to supply to
dsm() in your message. The data format for dsm is given in the
"?dsm-data" manual page.
  - Not sure whether this is a typo or not, but your distance column
should be named "distance" not "distance(m)"
  - If size=0, then you didn't observe anything? In that case you need
an entry in the segments data.frame but not for the observations (as
there were no observations there). Remember that the data setup is so
you have detections in the detection function object, effort in the
segments and then the observation frame links these.
  - Bear in mind that the DSM is only a correlative method, so you can't
say anything about causal mechanism between covariates and distribution.
Usual caveats apply.

3. Is the reason for including an s(x,y) term (as per the vignette

example) simply to allow for the geographical visualisation of the
response variable?

  - No. The smooth of x,y is a proper model term and will fit a smooth
of space. It's possible to build models without x,y and still plot them
(these are usually referred to as "habitat models" in the cetacean
literature).

4. Does the structure of my model formula correctly reflect the intended

nested structure of my data as a random effect?

  - This is a really complicated random effect to include just starting
out. I'd recommend fitting some simpler models to begin with to get a
feel for dsm, and your data. For example fitting without the random
effects or with just each random effect in turn.
  - consult ?mgcv::random.effects and ?smooth.construct.re.smooth.spec
for more details on conversion between lme-type random effects and mgcv.
There are more details in Simon Wood's 2017 GAM book.
  - you can set engine="gamm" and use the random=list(...) construct to
build your random effects in lme-style. This is almost completely
untested though. It's likely that there will be issues fitting such a
model as the PQL that underlies gamm is not as reliable as the rest of
the GAM machinery.

Hope this helps.

best,
--dave

Hi Brianna, hi listfolks,

We've not investigated using these zero-inflated distributions in dsm
yet and I don't know how well they are supported in the current
framework. Your best bet would be to use dsm to create the dataset, then
extract the $data column from the resulting model, then pass that back
to gam() to get started with ZIP.

That being said, I wonder what you are using to work out if the model is
working well. In general plots of observed vs. predicted per segment
will look bad because of the way that the smooths smudge out the
density. dsm provides obs_exp() which lets you compare the observed vs
expected over binned versions of the covariates (in the dsm or detection
function). So, for example, looking at obs vs. expected for different
Beaufort levels or bathymetric depth intervals may reveal the model is
doing well, once aggregated. An example output is given in
https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.07996 (see tables 3 and 4).

As it says in the mgcv::negbin manual page: "'gamm' does not support
'theta' estimation". There are a few options, one of which would be to
use a value of theta derived from a gam() fit to the same data using the
nb() response.

With both of these approaches (GAMM and ZIP) are starting to get fairly
complicated models with additional assumptions and additional fitting

which, involves some assumptions about how the system works.

messages.body_plain:
Dayrone

Welcome to the list.  It is not obvious from your question whether you are using the stand-alone Distance for Windows software  http://distancesampling.org/Distance/index.html , or the package called Distance that is run using R.  I speculate that you are using R, because Distance for Windows provides guidance on structuring data for input.  If I'm wrong, please write again and correct me.

By "replicates" I assume you mean transects.  We have several data sets online that you can examine to see how they are structured.  For example,
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/ducknests.csv consists of data from 20 transects, all of the same length, within a single stratum
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.csv contains data from 25 transects; 13 in stratum "South" and 12 in stratum "North".  In this dataset, there are a number of transects on which no detections were made.  Note how these are recorded.
For your second question regarding area.  The software does not need the value of a=2lw to perform its calculations.  The overlap between transects is not of great concern.  Consider an extreme case of overlap: each transect is walked twice.  That results in complete overlap of transects.  This is a common type of survey design, for example, when transects need to be cut. This poses no problem in analysis, as long as the effort associated with transects reflects the length is double the physical length of the transect.

I hope this is helpful.
